decisionGap: The guide is framed around employer plans and has no owner-only passage, while 'can i take a loan from a solo 401k' and related questions appear as autocomplete completions. Sampled the 2026-11-14 research pack and autocomplete export; no site-wide uniqueness claimed.
finding: A loan from an owner-only 401(k) follows the same 26 U.S.C. 72(p) limits, if the plan document provides for loans. A plan loan is lending between a plan and a disqualified person (4975(c)(1)(B)), and the 4975(d)(1) exemption needs five conditions: availability on a reasonably equivalent basis, no larger amounts for highly compensated employees, specific plan provisions, a reasonable interest rate and adequate security. Section 4975(f)(6) bars the (d) exemption for loans to IRA participants and to employers that establish IRAs, so an IRA-based plan cannot lend to its owner. A 5-percent owner is a key employee (416(i)(1)(A)(ii)), so interest on the owner's own loan is not deductible (72(p)(3)).
conditions: Federal statute only; the plan document and its administrator decide whether a given loan meets the conditions. No provider-specific claims. Not tax or legal advice.
whatWouldChange: A plan document without a loan provision, a loan that fails any of the five 4975(d)(1) conditions, a change in how a provider administers the plan, or a change to 26 U.S.C. 72(p), 4975 or 416(i).
whyNoQuantitativeAnalysis: The answer is a conditional legal rule read from statute text, not a computation; the calculator page on the same route family handles the numbers.
reasoning: 72(p)(1) treats a plan loan as a distribution unless 72(p)(2) applies; 72(p)(2) sets the same caps for every qualified plan. 4975(c)(1)(B) makes lending between a plan and a disqualified person a prohibited transaction; 4975(d)(1)(A)-(E) exempts a participant loan only when all five conditions hold; 4975(f)(6)(A)-(B) disables that exemption for owner-employees, and (B)(iii) limits the loan exclusion to IRA participants and IRA-establishing employers, so a solo 401(k) owner is not categorically barred while an IRA-based plan cannot lend to its owner. 416(i)(1)(A)(ii) makes a 5-percent owner a key employee, and 72(p)(3) denies the interest deduction for a key employee's loan.
